Chapter 4: The Biblical Foundation for Church Practices and the Call for Reform
When you start asking tough questions about things like indulgences, church authority, and how we find assurance in our faith, it naturally leads to something bigger.
How do we decide which church practices really matter—and which ones might need a second look?
The answer, honestly, is to go back to the basics: the teachings of the Bible. Scripture gives us the standard against which every tradition, custom, or new idea should be measured.
Over the centuries, the church has created all sorts of ways to help believers grow in faith. Some of these practices are clearly rooted in the Bible, while others have popped up as times changed.
The real challenge is figuring out which ones stay true to Christ’s message—and which, maybe, have drifted a bit from their original purpose.
Take the sale of indulgences, for example. If you hold it up to Scripture, it just doesn’t stack up. The Bible teaches that forgiveness is a gift from God—something we receive through faith and repentance, not by paying for it.
There’s no mention in Scripture about buying spiritual benefits or securing salvation with money. Instead, the focus is on humility, confession, and a true willingness to change.
And that’s where a biblical perspective really challenges us. It asks us to take a close, honest look at every church practice. If a tradition lines up with what Christ and the apostles taught, great—let’s keep it. But if it contradicts or clouds the core message of the Gospel, it’s time to rethink, reform, or even let it go.
This isn’t about throwing away the past. It’s about getting back to the heart of the Christian faith.
Reform, in this sense, isn’t rebellion. It’s actually a sign of loyalty to the truth. It means being willing to ask hard questions, listen to your conscience, and dig deeper into what God really wants for us. The point isn’t to split the church, but to make it stronger—by focusing on what matters most.
It takes both humility and courage. We have to admit that even well-meaning traditions can get off track. That’s why it’s so valuable to invite open conversations, honest debates, and shared discernment.
After all, the church is a community—a family of believers—meant to walk through this process together, always seeking God’s wisdom and guidance.
So, what does reform look like in everyday church life?
It could mean reviewing our current practices in light of Scripture and asking, “Does this actually help people grow in faith?”
It means encouraging open dialogue among church leaders, theologians, and everyone in the congregation—creating a culture of respect and learning.
It means putting the needs of the poor and vulnerable first, making sure the church’s resources are used to serve others—not to build up wealth.
Most of all, it means keeping our eyes on the core message of the Gospel: forgiveness, grace, and the invitation to live a changed life.
When the church roots its practices in Scripture and embraces the need to reform, it can renew its purpose and give the world a more genuine, powerful witness.
But remember, this isn’t a one-time thing. It’s an ongoing process—one that calls for vigilance, discernment, and a real openness to change.
It’s a journey of faith, guided by the light of God’s word and the example Jesus set for us.
